study_identification_part.si4_title: Brain charts for the human lifespan

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To create brain charts for the human lifespan using the largest aggregated neuroimaging dataset to date, establishing reference standards to quantify individual differences in brain structure across the lifespan from mid-gestation to 100 years of age.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Case-control differences analyzed with bootstrapped non-parametric generalization of Welch's one-way ANOVA; pairwise comparisons using Monte Carlo permutation tests (10,000 permutations) with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (q<0.05); Cohen's d effect sizes calculated; sex-stratified analyses; hierarchical clustering of multivariate centile profiles across disorders; associations with birth weight and gestational age tested via linear regression; twin-based heritability estimation; longitudinal stability assessed via IQR of centile scores; diagnostic progression analyses for MCI-to-AD conversion
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Brain charts revealed previously unreported neurodevelopmental milestones, showed high longitudinal stability, demonstrated robustness across studies, increased heritability of centile scores, and revealed distinct patterns of neuroanatomical variation across psychiatric and neurological disorders with Alzheimer's disease showing the greatest deviation from normative trajectories.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study created comprehensive brain charts spanning 115 days post-conception to 100 years using 123,984 scans from 101,457 participants across 100+ studies. Key milestones identified include: GMV peak at 5.9 years (95% CI 5.8-6.1), WMV peak at 28.7 years (95% CI 28.1-29.2), sGMV peak at 14.4 years (95% CI 14.0-14.7), and cortical thickness peak at 1.7 years (95% CI 1.3-2.1). An early GMV:WMV differentiation period was delineated from 1 month to 3 years post-birth. Case-control comparisons showed significant differences across disorders with effect sizes ranging from medium (Cohen's d 0.2-0.8) to large (d>0.8). Alzheimer's disease showed the greatest deviation (median centile 14%, 36 percentage points from control median, d=0.88 for GMV in females). Schizophrenia ranked third on multivariate CMD after AD and MCI. Centile scores showed increased heritability compared to raw volumes (average 11.8 percentage point increase in h²). Longitudinal centile IQR was low (<0.05) indicating high stability, with increased variability in individuals showing diagnostic progression. Birth weight and gestational age were significantly associated with adult centile scores (gestational age: t=13.164, P<2×10⁻¹⁶; birth weight: t=36.395, P<2×10⁻¹⁶). Leave-one-study-out analyses confirmed robustness, and out-of-sample centile scoring required N>100 for stability.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This landmark study represents the largest neuroimaging dataset aggregated to date for normative modeling (123,984 scans from 101,457 participants). The approach uses WHO-recommended GAMLSS framework adapted for multi-site neuroimaging with hierarchical random effects. A key innovation is the out-of-sample estimation procedure enabling application without data sharing. The study demonstrates that cross-sectional models show high longitudinal stability. The identified GMV:WMV differentiation period (birth to 3 years) represents a novel neurodevelopmental window not previously delineated. Regional analyses revealed heterochronicity in cortical development with sensory regions peaking earlier than association cortex, recapitulating known gradients. The centile approach is explicitly distinguished from brain age prediction, focusing on vertical (deviation from norm) rather than horizontal (age prediction) displacement. Increased heritability of centiled phenotypes suggests improved signal-to-noise for genetic studies. The study acknowledges it does not yet support individual clinical diagnosis but proves the principle at research scale. Supplementary materials contain extensive validation including comparison to brain weight, ultrasound, and head circumference data from external sources.
